title: How To Handle A Student Who Gets Angry When You Give Them A Consequence hen-you-give-them-a-consequence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the common early-year moment when a student reacts badly to a fairly given consequence — sighing, rolling eyes, complaining, or glaring — arguing this reaction is normal and not a sign the approach needs adjusting. He lays out three rules for enforcement: never wait for a reaction, delivering the consequence and immediately turning away so there's no one present to escalate at; never respond to theatrics unless the misbehavior crosses into blatant disrespect, since responding proves the enforcement is personal rather than procedural; and never waver, so that consistent, identical follow-through teaches students that arguing is pointless because the plan itself, not the teacher, is what's immovable. For cases of brazen disrespect (cursing, yelling), his advice is to show zero reaction in the moment, wait until the student calms down — possibly hours later — then approach and deliver a further consequence that must include parent contact.
points: Never wait for a student's reaction after giving a consequence — deliver it and immediately turn and walk away, leaving no one present to escalate at.
Don't respond to dramatic reactions (sighs, eye rolls, muttered complaints) unless the behavior crosses into blatant disrespect — responding proves it's personal.
Consistent, identical follow-through every time teaches students that arguing with you is pointless because it's the plan, not you, that is immovable.
For brazen disrespect like cursing or yelling, show zero reaction in the moment; wait until the student has fully calmed down, even hours later, before addressing it.
Any further consequence delivered after brazen disrespect has calmed down must include parent contact.
quotes: They sigh dramatically. They roll their eyes. They complain under their breath, glare at you, blame others, etc.

First, never wait for a reaction. The way we teach giving a consequence here at SCM is to approach, enforce (“You have a warning because you broke rule number two.”), and then turn on your heel and walk away.
Remaining in the student’s air space, on the other hand, especially if you’re looking at them, all but begs for a reaction—which some students will provide just to save face in front of their peers.
You’re as impenetrable as Edinburgh Castle. Your rules and consequences are set like an iron stake in frozen ground.
Ignore for now. Show zero reaction. Wait until they calm down, or even forget about the incident. It could be 10 minutes. It could be an hour.
Regardless, once they’re calm, approach and give further consequence, which absolutely has to include parent contact.
